findings.title: `prisma` is not imported
findings.body: This new `prisma.credential.update` call references `prisma`, but this file has no `prisma` import or declaration. TypeScript will report `Cannot find name 'prisma'`, preventing the app from type-checking or building.

findings.title: The sync branch returns a Fetch Response instead of token data
findings.body: When credential syncing is enabled, this returns the raw `fetch` Response, while the fallback returns each provider's native token result. Several callers expect token data directly or under `.data`: Google reads `res.data`, HubSpot reads `accessToken`/`expiresIn`, and Zoho Bigin/CRM read `tokenInfo.data`. A Fetch Response has none of those fields, so these integrations fail or persist malformed credentials when they use the sync endpoint. Decode and normalize the endpoint response to the contract expected by callers.

findings.title: The computed Zod keys do not match arbitrary response fields
findings.body: `z.string().toString()` produces a fixed property name, not a wildcard key matcher; both computed properties therefore refer to a fixed key, and the second overwrites the first. Zod strips unrecognized object properties by default, so synced responses lose fields such as `expires_in`, `expiry_date`, and `refresh_token`. For example, Zoom then receives no expiry and replaces its refresh token with the literal placeholder added below, while Office 365 retains a stale expiry and may refresh repeatedly.

findings.title: The SafeParse wrapper is stored as the credential key
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the result of `safeParse` (`{ success, data }`), but this code treats that result as the parsed key and saves it to `credential.key`. On the next Google auth attempt, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` receives the wrapper rather than the token fields and fails, leaving the user's Google Calendar credential unusable after a refresh.

findings.title: The connection uses the old access token after refreshing
findings.body: The code obtains and persists `accessTokenParsed.data`, but constructs the Salesforce connection with `credentialKey.access_token`, which is the pre-refresh token. If that token expired, the connection still uses an expired token and Salesforce API calls fail despite the refresh succeeding. Use the refreshed access token when constructing the connection.

findings.title: Salesforce refresh bypasses the credential sync endpoint
findings.body: Unlike the other adapters, this refresh path calls Salesforce directly and never uses `refreshOAuthTokens`. When credential syncing is enabled, Salesforce therefore continues using the locally stored refresh token instead of asking the configured source-of-truth endpoint for the user's refreshed credentials, so Salesforce does not support the feature this PR adds.

findings.title: Bigin sends a credential ID as the user ID
findings.body: The third argument is interpreted by `refreshOAuthTokens` as the Cal.com user ID and is sent as `calcomUserId`, but this call passes `credentialId` (the credential record ID). The sync endpoint will look up the wrong user, causing refresh failures or associating credentials with a different user if IDs happen to collide. Pass the credential's user ID instead.

findings.title: Zoom sync requests use the wrong app slug
findings.body: This sends `zoomvideo` as `appSlug`, but Zoom credentials are registered under the app slug `zoom` (for example, the callback creates credentials with `appId: "zoom"`). A sync endpoint that looks up the app by slug will not find the Zoom app, so token refresh fails. Pass the registered slug.
